Introduction time and spread of a resistance variant

This Vignette details the GeneCastR pipeline on sixteen Ugandan districts surveyed annually from 2016 to 2022 for the PfKelch13 C469Y artemisinin-resistance marker.

library(GeneCastR)

The model

We model in discrete time with M steps per unit of time, in our running example one unit of time is equal to one year, with \(M=16\) steps per year. We denote the allele count at time \(t\) with \(k_t\) and set \(k_0=0\), meaning that the focal allele is yet to be imported at initialisation.

We denote the first arrival time with t*. The arrival event occurs with constant hazard theta per unit time, so that \(t^* \sim Geometric(1-\exp\{-\theta/M\})\). At t* the deme receives a founding count drawn from Poisson(lambda) conditioned on being non-zero, where \(\lambda \geq 0\).

From t* onward \(k_t\) follows the following Wright-Fisher dynamics

$$k_{t+1} \mid k_t \sim \mathrm{Binomial}\!\left(N_{\mathrm{lat}},\; \frac{f_t(1+\alpha)}{1+\alpha f_t}\right), \qquad f_t = k_t/N_{\mathrm{lat}},$$

if \(k_t\geq 1\), and \(k_{t+1}\sim Poi(\lambda)\) if \(k_t=0\). This means that a lineage can die out and the deme be re-founded, any number of times.

Observation surveys are modelled as binomial samples. Given a latent frequency \(f_t=k_t/N_{\mathrm{lat}}\) at time \(t\), a survey of \(n\) gene copies is assumed to follow \(x_t \sim Binomial(n, f_t)\).

Parameterisation

The parameters are all cast as per unit time to allow for different choices of time resolution \(M\). Each is transformed so that it has a ‘per year’ interpretation invariant to M, summarised in the table below; the rest of this section says why each transform has the form it does.

parameter meaning support state-space quantity transform
A growth advantage per unit time A > -1 alpha, selection per step alpha = (1 + A)^(1/M) - 1
nu gene flow, in frequency units per unit time nu > 0 lambda, Poisson mean per step lambda = nu * N_eff
N_eff effective size, in gene copies N_eff > 0 N_lat, lattice size in copies N_lat = max(2, round(M * N_eff))
theta hazard of founding, per unit time theta > 0 p, founding chance per step p = 1 - exp(-theta / M)

A growth advantage of A over a unit of time is M steps of alpha, so (1 + alpha)^M = 1 + A. Sampling is done on u = log(1 + A), which makes alpha = exp(u/M) - 1.

N_lat is linear in both M and N_eff Binomial sampling gives the frequency a variance of f(1-f)/N_lat in one step. Over the M steps in a year that accumulates to M * f(1-f) / N_lat, and setting it equal to f(1-f)/N_eff – the drift of a single Wright-Fisher generation in a population of N_eff – forces N_lat = M * N_eff.

drift_per_year <- function(M, N_eff = 15.6, f = 0.3, N_lat = NULL) {
  nl <- if (is.null(N_lat)) gc_nlat(log(N_eff), M) else N_lat
  P <- gc_kernel(nl, 0)                       # neutral
  k <- round(f * nl); g <- (0:nl) / nl
  mean_f <- sum(P[k + 1L, ] * g)
  M * sum(P[k + 1L, ] * (g - mean_f)^2)       # variance per step, times M
}
c(M8 = drift_per_year(8), M16 = drift_per_year(16),
  M32 = drift_per_year(32), M128 = drift_per_year(128),
  target = 0.3 * 0.7 / 15.6)
#>         M8        M16        M32       M128     target 
#> 0.01354138 0.01344000 0.01348233 0.01345891 0.01346154

Hold N_lat fixed instead and a year’s worth of drift doubles every time the step halves:

vapply(c(8, 16, 32, 64), drift_per_year, numeric(1), N_lat = 250L)
#> [1] 0.00672 0.01344 0.02688 0.05376

Two parameters are moved on a log scale, because both are positive and neither is bounded above: u = log(1 + A) and z = log N_eff. These are the names the sampler’s internals and its diagnostics use – accept_z and step_z in fit$info are the z block’s – while the draws come back on the scale with a meaning, as A and N_eff[d].

A and N_eff are shared across the demes by default, which is the fit presented below. gc_control() will give either one a per-deme version: neff = "hierarchical" draws each z_d from N(mu, sigma^2), so mu and sigma are the mean and spread of the log effective size across demes, and selection = "hierarchical" draws each u_d from N(mu_u, sigma_u^2), mu_u and sigma_u being the same two for the log growth advantage. Both spreads carry priors whose mode is at zero, so a per-deme version can collapse back onto the shared one rather than being held apart by the prior. theta, for its part, is given an Exponential(rate) prior with rate defaulting to the length of the observation window.

The panel-level size is named for the structure that was fitted. Under the shared default there is one size and nothing to average over, so it comes back as N_eff, with its log as log_N_eff. Under neff = "hierarchical" the same slot instead holds the exponential of the mean log size, which describes a typical deme rather than any particular one, and is reported as exp_mu with mu beneath it. sigma is not a parameter under the shared default and is reported as NA.

N_lat is an integer, because it counts gene copies, so the likelihood is piecewise constant in N_eff: two values that round to the same lattice give exactly the same model. Rounding is half-to-even, and the floor of 2 is there because a lattice of 0 or 1 has no interior for drift or selection to act on.

The invariance is close but not exact: the full likelihood still shifts by about 0.6 nats between M = 16 and M = 32, and 1.8 nats across the whole range from M = 8 to M = 64. M = 16 is the resolution the stored fit uses.

The shared-parameter model in full

Collecting the above, with the defaults of gc_control(), for a panel of \(D\) demes observed over \(T\) steps at \(M\) steps per unit of time. One growth advantage, one effective size, one flow rate and one hazard serve the whole panel; each deme keeps its own arrival time and its own path.

Priors, written on the scale the sampler moves:

$$u = \log(1+A) \sim N(0, \tau^2), \qquad \tau = 1,$$ $$z = \log N_{\mathrm{eff}} \sim N(\mu_0, s_0^2), \qquad \mu_0 = \log 15,\; s_0 = 1.5,$$ $$\nu \sim \mathrm{HalfNormal}(0.02), \qquad \theta \sim \mathrm{Exponential}(\mathrm{span}).$$

Transforms onto the lattice:

$$\alpha = e^{u/M} - 1, \qquad N_{\mathrm{lat}} = \max\{2, \mathrm{round}(M e^{z})\}, \qquad \lambda = \nu e^{z}, \qquad p = 1 - e^{-\theta/M}.$$

Then for each deme \(d = 1, \dots, D\) independently, an arrival time, a founding count and a path:

$$t^*_d \sim \mathrm{Geometric}(p) \;\text{ on } \{1, 2, \dots\}, \qquad k_{d,0} = \dots = k_{d,\,t^*_d - 1} = 0,$$ $$k_{d,\,t^*_d} \sim \mathrm{Poisson}(\lambda) \mid {\geq 1}, \qquad k_{d,\,t^*_d:T} \sim \mathrm{WF}(\alpha, N_{\mathrm{lat}}, \lambda),$$

where \(\mathrm{WF}\) is one draw of the path given above: a \(\mathrm{Binomial}(N_{\mathrm{lat}}, \psi(f_t, \alpha))\) step while the deme holds a copy and a \(\mathrm{Poisson}(\lambda)\) re-entry while it is empty. The selection tilt is \(\psi(f, \alpha) = f(1+\alpha) / (1 + \alpha f)\), the frequency written in the Binomial above: it carries \(f\) upwards whenever \(\alpha > 0\) and fixes \(\psi(0,\alpha) = 0\), \(\psi(1,\alpha) = 1\), so neither absence nor fixation is disturbed by selection. Finally each survey \(j\) in deme \(d\), taken at step \(s_{dj}\) and typing \(n_{dj}\) gene copies,

$$x_{dj} \sim \mathrm{Binomial}\!\left(n_{dj},\; k_{d,\,s_{dj}}/N_{\mathrm{lat}}\right).$$

Four details of that generative story are worth stating, because they are places the implementation could have cut a corner and does not.

The arrival time is not a sampled quantity. It is summed out exactly in the same backward pass that evaluates the likelihood, so its posterior is a normalisation of a row already computed and carries no Monte-Carlo error.

\(\mathrm{Geometric}(p)\) is unbounded, so \(P(t^* > T) = e^{-\theta \cdot \mathrm{span}}\) is positive: a deme may simply not have been reached yet, and a deme never seen positive is not forced to have been reached and then hidden.

The founding draw is conditioned on being non-zero, while the re-entry draw is not – an empty deme stays empty with probability \(e^{-\lambda}\). Both are truncated at \(N_{\mathrm{lat}}\) with the tail folded onto the last cell, so each row sums to one rather than leaking mass.

For the running example \(D = 16\), \(M = 16\), \(\mathrm{span} = 12\) years and so \(T = 192\) steps.

In the next sections we explain how to use the package to infer model parameters, including selection, effective population size, and importation time.

Data

Input is one row per survey.

d <- gc_example_data(M = 16)
#> 16 row(s) with n == 0 dropped (no information).
d
#> <GCData>
#>   demes    : 16 (Agago, Amolatar, Arua, ...)
#>   surveys  : 96 (42 non-zero)
#>   window   : 2015 to 2022   M = 16, T = 112 steps
#>   never positive: 2 deme(s) -- Jinja, Kanungu

The window printed there is the default: t0 sits one unit of time before the first survey. Where the window opens is a prior claim about the earliest possible arrival rather than anything the data say, so it is made at fit time instead – see lead_in below.

Fitting

Parameter posteriors can be drawn using a Metropolis-within-Gibbs scheme in which the true likelihood is evaluated exactly. An example fit output looks like this.

stored <- gc_example_fit()
fit <- stored$fit
fit
#> <GCFit>  Poisson flow, t* geometric (may postdate the record)
#>           (t* = the first non-zero draw)
#>   data    : 16 demes, 96 surveys, M = 16, T = 192
#>   window  : 2010 to 2022, lead-in 96 steps
#>   chains  : 4 x 4000 (2000 warm-up), 8000 draws retained
#>   time    : 3347.7 s on 4 cores
#> 
#>           variable  median      q5     q95 rhat ess_bulk
#>                  u  0.1495 -0.1421  0.3705 1.01      877
#>                  A  0.1612 -0.1325  0.4484 1.01      877
#>                 nu  0.0255  0.0111  0.0472 1.00      903
#>              N_eff 15.6002  7.9211 30.0540 1.01      866
#>              theta  0.1804  0.1063  0.3233 1.00     1199
#>  p_beyond_baseline  0.1148  0.0207  0.2792 1.00     1199

To produce such a fit given data d with default priors we can run:

fit <- GCFit$new(d, chains = 4, iter = 4000, warmup = 2000, seed = 101,
                 cores = 4, lead_in = 6 * 16, control = gc_control(selection = "shared"))

lead_in is the lead-in before the first survey, counted in steps, so 6 * 16 is six years at M = 16 and puts t0 in 2010. It is the earliest arrival the model will allow. A t* posterior piled up against t0 is the sign that a lead-in is too short to hold the arrival it is being asked to date. gc_control allows users to modify priors and model hierarchical structure, see the appendix for a description of functionality; for default use, omit the argument.

Once complete, one can plot parameter mcmc traces:

gc_plot_trace(fit)

The same draws as histograms, with the chains kept apart. Disagreement between chains shows here as displaced humps, which a shared histogram hides.

gc_plot_hist(fit)

Pairwise, to tell a ridge – two parameters the data cannot separate – from one parameter merely absorbing signal from another:

gc_plot_pairs(fit)

Nothing here is a ridge, but the largest correlation is not negligible either: 0.42 between u and N_eff. With one effective size for the whole panel, selection and drift are inferred from the same sixteen trajectories and do trade against each other. Neither is unidentified, but the growth advantage should not be read as independent of the size.

N_eff is the one effective size the whole panel shares, this being the default. gc_control(neff = "hierarchical") gives each deme its own instead, drawn from N(mu, sigma^2); sigma then becomes a parameter, the panel level is reported as exp_mu, and gc_plot_trace(fit, "N_eff") has sixteen traces to show rather than one.

The growth advantage

u is what the sampler moves, but A = exp(u) - 1 is the quantity with a meaning: the proportional change in frequency per year that selection buys.

gc_plot_hist(fit, "A", ncol = 1)


A <- as.numeric(posterior::as_draws_matrix(fit$draws)[, "A"])
round(stats::quantile(A, c(.025, .05, .25, .5, .75, .95, .975)), 3)
#>   2.5%     5%    25%    50%    75%    95%  97.5% 
#> -0.176 -0.132  0.042  0.161  0.278  0.448  0.510

c(`P(A > 0)` = mean(A > 0), `P(A > 0.25)` = mean(A > 0.25))
#>    P(A > 0) P(A > 0.25) 
#>    0.824375    0.293500

The posterior favours a positive advantage without excluding neutrality: about a sixth of its mass lies below zero. Two things to hold alongside that: every district here is one where C469Y was observed, and conditioning of that kind inflates apparent selection; and the flow term competes with selection to explain late-appearing demes, so A is not identified independently of nu.

Acceptance rates and the guard counts are in fit$info. The N_eff bounds are rejections applied before the likelihood is evaluated: they stop a wild proposal allocating a vast lattice, and the rejections they generate are the negative feedback that keeps step-size adaptation stable.

fit$info[, c("chain", "accept_z", "accept_u", "accept_nu", "guard_rejects")]
#>   chain accept_z accept_u accept_nu guard_rejects
#> 1     1   0.2460   0.3175    0.2960           488
#> 2     2   0.2960   0.2785    0.2455           344
#> 3     3   0.3050   0.2820    0.3745           289
#> 4     4   0.2905   0.3075    0.3360           424

Projections

pr <- stored$pr
pr
#> <GCProjection>
#>   3840 rows: 16 demes x 240 steps (192 smoothed, 48 projected)
#>   window   : 2010.062 to 2025
#>   draws    : 200, 400 paths each
#>   exceedance thresholds: 0.01, 0.05, 0.1
#>   P(t* beyond the record): mean 0.074, max 0.627
#> 
#>   at 2025: mean P(present) 0.807, mean median f 0.090

pr <- fit$project(horizon = 3, n_draws = 200, n_paths = 400,
                  thresholds = c(0.01, 0.05, 0.10))

pr$curves is one row per deme and step.

names(pr$curves)
#>  [1] "deme"            "step"            "time"            "phase"          
#>  [5] "f_mean"          "f_q2.5"          "f_q25"           "f_q50"          
#>  [9] "f_q75"           "f_q97.5"         "p_present"       "p_present_q2.5" 
#> [13] "p_present_q50"   "p_present_q97.5" "p_exceed_1"      "p_exceed_5"     
#> [17] "p_exceed_10"     "pmf_tfirst"      "cdf_tfirst"      "pmf_test"       
#> [21] "cdf_test"

Inside the window these are smoothed: every survey in the deme, later ones included, informs the state at each step. Beyond the last survey the same kernel propagates the smoothed lattice distribution forward.

gc_plot_frequency(pr)

Two distinctions in that table are easy to lose and both matter.

f_q* are predictive; p_present_q* are not. The frequency quantiles integrate the parameters, the latent path and the Wright-Fisher noise, so f_q97.5 is a bound on the frequency itself. The presence quantiles hold the parameters out: they say how well the data pin a probability, not how uncertain the outcome is. Presence is a Bernoulli whose probability is itself uncertain, and the across-draw spread is only part of that variance.

The f_* columns are unconditional. The atom at zero carries 1 - p_present, so a quantile below that level is exactly zero, and a band resting on zero means absence is the likelier state rather than a frequency near zero.

gc_plot_present(pr)

P(present) is not monotone. It dips between surveys and recovers at each non-zero one, because a deme can go extinct and be re-seeded. Under a single introduction it could only ever rise.

Exceedance is computed on the lattice for every draw rather than from a binned density: the threshold falls between lattice points and the binning error does not average out.

gc_plot_exceed(pr)

Introduction times

Three times, and they are not interchangeable.

t* is a parameter, obtained analytically: the backward table is already built for the likelihood, so its posterior is a normalisation of a row that has already been computed, with no Monte-Carlo error at all.

T_first is the first step the variant is present. In this model the founding event deposits a copy at t* and nothing is present before it, so T_first is identically t*. Computing it from sampled paths anyway is a check that the two routes agree.

T_est is the start of the excursion that produced the first count anyone actually saw: walk back from the first survey with a non-zero reading until the deme is empty. It is a path functional – no marginal of the smoother says when that excursion began – so it needs sampled paths, and it is the only expensive output here. It is undefined in a deme that was never detected, there being no observed lineage to date, and it does not condition on survival: the lineage that was seen need not be the one still present at the end.

gc_plot_times(pr, "cdf")

Both curves reach one, and both stop at the dashed line – the first detection. That line is a hard bound: the excursion carrying the detected copy must have begun before the copy was seen.

The gap between the curves is the span over which earlier arrivals came and went before the one that was eventually caught. Where the two nearly coincide, as in Lamwo, the variant was detected soon after it arrived and there was no room for turnover. Where purple stays flat for years while green climbs, as in Arua or Rukiga, the variant very probably arrived long before the lineage that was actually seen, and whatever came first died out.

The two never-detected demes have no purple curve at all.

The same two quantities as densities, which show where the mass actually is rather than where it has accumulated. Densities are per unit time, so both are on one scale whatever M is, and each integrates to one in a deme that was detected.

gc_plot_times(pr, "pmf")

Multiple modes in a T_est density are successive extinction and recolonisation cycles, each one a plausible era for the founding of the lineage that was detected.

Every sampled path carries both times, so their joint distribution comes for free and is kept in pr$joint. Its diagonal is the probability that the lineage which was detected is the one that originally arrived – a quantity neither marginal can give, since both are compatible with either history. gc_plot_joint() draws it.

J <- pr$joint
share <- vapply(seq_along(pr$demes$deme),
                function(k) sum(diag(J[, , k])), numeric(1)) /
         pmax(pr$demes$p_alive_T, 1e-12)
round(sort(stats::setNames(share, pr$demes$deme), decreasing = TRUE), 2)
#>     Lamwo   Mubende  Amolatar     Hoima      Kole    Tororo     Agago   Katakwi 
#>      0.14      0.14      0.12      0.11      0.10      0.09      0.08      0.08 
#>   Kaabong      Arua    Kasese    Rukiga    Koboko Kapchorwa     Jinja   Kanungu 
#>      0.08      0.08      0.07      0.06      0.05      0.04      0.00      0.00

So in most demes the variant that was detected is not descended from the first arrival: the original lineage died out and a later one founded what was eventually seen.

Cost

The fit is the expensive part; everything after it is seconds.

one likelihood evaluation, 16 demes, M = 16, T = 192 10 ms
4 x 4000 sweeps, 4 cores 3348 s
projection, 200 draws ~9 s
path sampling, 400 paths per deme per draw ~45 s

The fit time is read back off the stored object rather than written down, so the table cannot drift away from the fit the rest of this vignette shows. It is one run on one laptop, and it moves with the machine and with whatever else that machine was doing at the time; the per-evaluation cost above is the figure to scale from.

n_paths = 0 skips the path sampler, which is the fast path: t* is analytic and costs nothing, and T_est is the only expensive output.

Cost grows as the square of the lattice, so M = 32 is about five times M = 16, and the per-sweep time is lumpy: the posterior for N_eff has a long right tail, and the largest draws cost many times what the median one does. Asking for per-deme sizes with gc_control(neff = "hierarchical") makes that worse, because each deme then draws its own lattice and a single wide one slows the whole sweep.

The N_eff guard rejects about a tenth of the z proposals, and most of that is at the lower bound – 0.086 against 0.015 at the upper one. The adapted step is 1.45 against a posterior spread of 0.40 in log N_eff, so a step that is efficient for sampling routinely overshoots below N_eff = 2. Rejecting those before the likelihood is evaluated is what stops a wild proposal allocating a vast lattice, and it costs nothing, because the rejection happens before any work.

Appendix: gc_control()

gc_control() carries everything about the model that is not the data: the priors, which parameters are shared across demes and which are not, what t* means, and the sampler’s own step sizes. It returns a plain list, named exactly as its arguments are, so a setting can be read back under the name it was passed and one object can serve several fits.

ctl <- gc_control(selection = "hierarchical", mu_mean = log(30), tau = 0.5)
ctl$mu_mean
#> [1] 3.401197

fit <- GCFit$new(d, chains = 4, iter = 4000, cores = 4, lead_in = 6 * 16,
                 control = ctl)

Anything left unnamed keeps its default, so gc_control() on its own is the model this vignette presents. The structural arguments come first because they decide which of the prior arguments mean anything at all.

argument what it sets active in
neff one effective size for the panel ("shared") or one per deme shrunk toward mu ("hierarchical") always
selection one growth advantage for the panel ("shared") or one per deme shrunk toward mu_u ("hierarchical") always
tstar "geometric", so t* may postdate the record, or "uniform" over the window always
founding what t* is: the first non-zero draw ("conditional"), a single copy ("one"), or the onset of the arrival rate ("rate") always
tau N(0, tau^2) on u = log(1 + A) always, but on different things: the shared u, or mu_u under "hierarchical"
u_bounds rejection bounds on u always
nu_scale HalfNormal(nu_scale) on the flow rate nu always
lognu_bounds rejection bounds on log nu always
mu_mean, mu_sd N(mu_mean, mu_sd^2) on the single z = log N_eff when neff = "shared", on mu when "hierarchical"
neff_bounds rejection bounds on N_eff, applied before the likelihood always
sigma2_shape, sigma2_rate InvGamma on sigma^2, the between-deme variance of z only neff = "hierarchical"
u_sigma_scale, u_sigma_df half-t on sigma_u, the between-deme spread of u only selection = "hierarchical"
tstar_rate rate of the Exponential prior on theta; NULL uses the window span only tstar = "geometric"
lntheta_bounds rejection bounds on log theta only tstar = "geometric"
target acceptance rate the warm-up adaptation aims at always
step_z, step_u, step_nu starting random-walk scales always

Three things that table is trying to make plain.

Four prior arguments are inert unless you ask for the structure they belong to. Setting sigma2_shape under the default neff = "shared" changes nothing, because there is no between-deme variance to put a prior on; the same goes for u_sigma_scale away from selection = "hierarchical", and for tstar_rate under tstar = "uniform". Nothing warns you, so it is worth checking fit$control against what you meant.

The bounds are rejections, not densities. A proposal outside them is refused before the likelihood is evaluated, which is what stops a wild draw from allocating a vast lattice, and the refusals are also the negative feedback that keeps step-size adaptation stable. They are not part of the model in the way the priors are, and a posterior pressed against one is a sign the bound is wrong rather than that the data have spoken.

A parameter the chosen structure does not have is either absent from fit$draws or present and NA, and which of the two depends on the parameter. sigma and log_sigma2 are always there, and are NA unless neff = "hierarchical". Everything else comes and goes:

in fit$draws only when variables
neff = "shared" N_eff, log_N_eff (otherwise exp_mu, mu)
tstar = "geometric" theta, p_beyond_baseline
selection = "hierarchical" u[d], A[d], mu_u, sigma_u

fit$summary() and the plotting functions consult fit$control and show only what the fit actually has, which is why the default reports six variables and never an empty sigma panel. posterior::variables(fit$draws) is the way to see the full set.

Defaults, with their justifications, are on the help page: ?gc_control.
